conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You’re here because of severe nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up feeling nauseous and started vomiting—like 10 times in an hour. It was dark but not bloody. I only ate a muffin for breakfast, nothing unusual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Any belly pain, fever, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No belly pain or fever, but my chest and upper stomach hurt a bit from all the retching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. In the ER, your blood pressure was high and heart rate fast, likely from dehydration. We’ve started IV fluids and anti-nausea meds like Compazine and Reglan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take domperidone for this. Why aren’t I getting it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Domperidone isn’t available here, and we couldn’t get it brought in. So we’re using Reglan instead, which works similarly to help your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I hope it works. I’ve had this before with my gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your symptoms match your usual flares. We’re also managing your diabetes with insulin through the IV fluids to keep your sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been hard to control lately. Is that making this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We found ketones in your urine, which means your body’s burning fat for energy. That can worsen nausea. That’s why we’re giving you dextrose in the IV—to help stop that process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. Did my blood sugar come down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 139 when you arrived, which is okay, but we’re watching closely. We adjusted your insulin sliding scale to keep it steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My blood pressure’s usually high too. Is that being treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since you couldn’t take pills, we gave IV metoprolol. Now that your vomiting’s slowing, we’ll switch back to your oral meds—metoprolol and lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my esophagitis? I’ve been on esomeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still getting your PPI—esomeprazole—daily. It helps with acid reflux, which can sometimes worsen nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but not vomiting as much. Maybe 2–3 times overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s improvement. Your labs show no infection—white count is normal. We also checked your A1c—it’s 7.2%, which is better than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been trying to manage it better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also sent a urine test for porphyria because of your repeated episodes. It came back negative, so that’s not the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pheochromocytoma test? I remember we talked about that last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent plasma metanephrines because your blood pressure was high with symptoms. But the 24-hour urine collection was incomplete—you didn’t follow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to collect it all. Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we can’t fully rule out pheo. We’ll discuss it with your GI doctor at follow-up. For now, we’ll focus on getting you stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination—no infection needing antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not for this. Your symptoms are from gastroparesis, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my breathing? I felt some crackling in my chest yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray yesterday. It’s unchanged—no pneumonia or fluid. Your Port-A-Cath and gastric pacer leads are in place. The crackles likely resolved with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Can I try eating something small?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with ice chips and see how you do. If no vomiting, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through the night with clear liquids. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had broth and juice, no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll try a soft diet today—maybe a saltine or toast. If that goes well, you might be ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great news. I was worried this would take longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve responded well. We’ll keep monitoring, but things are looking positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You tolerated a full meal last night—no nausea or vomiting. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes! I had mashed potatoes and chicken. Felt normal for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll discharge you today. You’ll go home on all your usual meds—domperidone, insulin, blood pressure pills, and PPI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Continue domperidone three times a day, insulin as per your sliding scale, and the rest as before. Use Compazine or Zofran if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up with GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep your scheduled appointment. They’ll review the pheo testing and your overall gastroparesis management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I worry about the incomplete urine test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The GI team will decide if it needs to be repeated. Focus on staying hydrated and eating small, frequent meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. A nurse will review everything with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep using the scopolamine patch as prescribed. It can help with nausea between flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I forgot to put one on before this episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might have contributed. Try to stay consistent, especially if you feel a flare coming on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you at follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The nurse will be in shortly with your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feel free to call your doctor if symptoms return or worsen after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to help you avoid that. Keep up with your diabetes care and GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your prescriptions sent to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.
